whyThisMatters: A lot of what feels true about handling tickets, calls, and alerts is only partly right — and IT Support is targeted precisely because attackers expect you to trust the routine parts of your own job. A few minutes here will clear up what really matters when a caller, a ticket, or an alert already looks familiar.
rememberThis: This month's reminder: familiar packaging is not proof. A ticket number, a caller who knows the jargon, or an alert styled like your own tool can all be faked — check the actual channel and domain every time, no matter how routine the request looks.

discussionPrompts: Ask if anyone has ever skipped part of the identity-verification process because the caller sounded senior or in a hurry. What made it hard to insist on the full check?
For the remote-access myth, ask how the team currently decides when it's okay to install a remote-access tool for someone calling in.
Ask honestly: does being on the IT team make people feel less likely to be targeted — and is that feeling actually true?
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People most often get the caller-ID myth wrong. A caller ID or display name looking right feels like real proof, so many people say it's safe to trust. But both can be spoofed just as easily as an email sender name — the only real check is a callback on a number you already had before the call.

items.myth: I can always tell a spoofed caller ID or a faked support email just by looking at it.
items.fact: Caller ID and display names can both be faked convincingly. The real check is calling back on a number you already had before the call, or checking the actual email domain letter by letter — not what is displayed on screen.
items.detail: A vendor-impersonation call often uses a caller ID that looks exactly like the real support line. Treat every unexpected support call the same way you'd treat an unexpected email: verify through a channel you already trust, never one the caller supplies.

items.myth: If a caller or email already knows our internal ticket number, it must be genuine.
items.fact: A ticket number can be observed, guessed, or picked up from an earlier compromised message. Knowing the number is not the same as being the genuine requester.
items.detail: Always confirm an escalation against the actual ticket queue yourself, and check that the request's contents (not just the number) match what's really in the system, before acting on it.

items.myth: MFA or password-reset requests over the phone are fine as long as the caller can answer a couple of internal-sounding questions.
items.fact: Attackers gather internal jargon and details from breached data, public sources, or earlier calls. Sounding convincing is not the same as passing your team's actual identity-verification process.
items.detail: The verification steps exist for exactly this reason — follow the same process every time, regardless of how urgent or senior the caller sounds. A genuine requester will not mind the check.

items.myth: IT staff are less likely to be targeted, because we already know the tricks.
items.fact: Attackers specifically target IT and admin accounts because they open more doors than a normal account. Training does not remove the pressure tactics — it means the habit matters even more for this team.
items.detail: Admin credentials, remote-access tools, and escalation privileges make IT Support a higher-value target, not a lower-risk one. The same STOP, VERIFY, REPORT habit applies here, not an exception to it.

items.myth: A system alert that looks exactly like our own monitoring tool's style must really be from that tool.
items.fact: The visual style, logo, and layout of an internal tool are easy for an attacker to copy. A genuine alert never asks you to re-enter your password through a link, no matter how authentic it looks.
items.detail: Check any urgent-looking system alert by opening the tool's own console directly yourself, rather than clicking through the alert — the look of the message proves nothing about where it actually came from.

items.myth: Installing a remote-access tool to help a caller quickly is fine, since IT installs and removes tools like this all the time.
items.fact: Installing remote access for an unverified caller gives them the same access you have. The fact that this is routine for IT is exactly why the trick blends in so easily.
items.detail: Treat any request to install a remote-access tool for an inbound caller the same as any other high-privilege action: verify who is actually asking, through a channel you already trust, before you install anything.
